```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Forecasting causes of death one at a time gives cause-specific forecasts
that do not add up to the all-cause forecast. mortensor offers two remedies:

* `cause_shares()` models all-cause mortality with any model and the shares
  of the causes with a compositional tensor model (isometric log-ratio
  coordinates and a Tucker decomposition across age, year, group and cause),
  so causes add up to all causes in every draw;
* `mt_reconcile()` adjusts independent forecasts draw by draw so that they
  add up (MinT, WLS or OLS projection).

The Human Mortality Database has no causes of death, so this vignette uses
`mt_example_causes()`: simulated deaths of women and men by cause
(cardiovascular disease, cancer, other) with known shares that change with
age and time.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_example_causes(years = 1990:2019)
x
mt_validate(x, hierarchy = list(var = "cause", total = "all"))
```

`mt_validate()` with a hierarchy checks that the causes add up to all
causes; in real data this check catches problems such as doubled totals.

## Cause shares

Shares of rare causes at young ages are noisy. Smoothing the cause-specific
rates first (`step_smooth()`, Poisson P-splines over age) keeps that noise
out of the share model; without it the forecast intervals of the causes were
too wide in the backtest below (95% coverage above 0.99).

```{r}
prep <- mt_prep(step_smooth())
fit <- mt_fit(cause_shares(total = lee_carter(), ranks = c(3, 3, 2, 2)), x, prep = prep)
fit$diagnostics
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
st <- fc$strata
coherence_gap <- function(fc, sx) {
  i <- st$stratum[st$sex == sx & st$cause == "all"]
  j <- st$stratum[st$sex == sx & st$cause != "all"]
  max(abs(apply(fc$rates[, , j, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 2, 4), sum) / fc$rates[, , i, ] - 1))
}
c(female = coherence_gap(fc, "female"), male = coherence_gap(fc, "male"))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_forecast(fc, ages = c("50", "70", "85"), strata = c("male.all", "male.cvd", "male.cancer", "male.other"))
```

## Independent forecasts and reconciliation

Independent Lee-Carter fits per cause do not add up:

```{r}
fc_ind <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x, prep = prep), h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
c(female = coherence_gap(fc_ind, "female"), male = coherence_gap(fc_ind, "male"))
fc_rec <- mt_reconcile(fc_ind, var = "cause", total = "all", method = "mint")
c(female = coherence_gap(fc_rec, "female"), male = coherence_gap(fc_rec, "male"))
```

## Backtest by cause

```{r}
origins <- 2005:2009
bt <- rbind(
  mt_backtest(cause_shares(total = lee_carter(), ranks = c(3, 3, 2, 2)), x, origins = origins, h = 10,
              n_draws = 200, prep = prep),
  mt_backtest(lee_carter(), x, origins = origins, h = 10, n_draws = 200, prep = prep))
mt_score(bt, by = c("model", "cause"))[order(cause, crps)]
```

The cause-share model borrows strength across ages, years, sexes and causes
for the composition, while all-cause mortality keeps its own model. Which
approach forecasts better depends on the data; the backtest above is the way
to decide.
